intro: Seattle's most famous silhouette began as a doodle on a napkin in 1959 and rose 605 feet in 400 days. This is how a World's Fair tower became the permanent symbol of the Space Age.
page_title: Space Needle: Exploded 3D Model and History | Architectural Atlas

sections.body: In 1959, hotel executive Edward E. Carlson sketched a tower on a napkin: a restaurant floating above Seattle like a flying saucer. Architect John Graham and Company turned the doodle into a buildable design, with structural engineer John K. Minasian working out how three legs could carry a 42-meter-wide top house 184 meters in the air. Construction started on 17 April 1961 and finished on 8 December 1961, about 400 days later, just in time for the Century 21 Exposition. The tower opened to the public on 21 April 1962, the first day of the fair, whose theme was The Age of Space. The Needle was the theme made concrete and steel.
sections.heading: A napkin sketch for the Space Age

sections.body: The 605-foot height was no accident: it is exactly twice the 300-foot width of the base, a proportion the designers chose for visual balance. Three tapering legs splay wide at the ground, pinch to a narrow waist about two-thirds of the way up, then flare again to carry the saucer. The whole structure weighs 9,550 tons, and the foundation alone accounts for 5,850 of them: a pit 30 feet deep, filled in under 12 hours by 467 cement trucks, with 72 anchor bolts tying the tower down. The center of gravity sits only about five feet above the ground. It is engineered to withstand 200 mph winds and a 9.0 magnitude earthquake.
sections.heading: Twice as tall as its footprint

sections.body: The top house holds two levels. The observation deck sits at 520 feet, reached by glass elevators that climb the outside of the core at 10 mph and arrive in 41 seconds. Below it, at 500 feet, the SkyCity restaurant measures 94.5 feet across and originally revolved once every 47 minutes on a 125-ton turntable driven by a 1.5 horsepower motor. The 2018 Century Project renovation gave the deck floor-to-ceiling glass and replaced the restaurant with The Loupe, the world's first revolving glass floor, looking straight down 500 feet to the ground.
sections.heading: The saucer at 520 feet

sections.body: The 1962 paint scheme carried the Space Age theme into the color chart: Astronaut White for the legs, Re-entry Red for the halo, Orbital Olive for the core, and Galaxy Gold for the sunburst and roof. The tower has been repainted many times since, and today it wears white with an orange-red top that recalls the original. The roof carries 25 lightning rods. On 19 April 1999 the city's Landmarks Preservation Board designated the tower a historic landmark. It now welcomes over one million visitors a year, and an American flag flies from the top.
sections.heading: Galaxy Gold and Re-entry Red

sections.body:
Nora Ephron's Sleepless in Seattle (1993) rooted its story in the city with shots of Pike Place Market and the Space Needle, and the tower has been a pilgrimage site for fans ever since. Here is the wrinkle worth knowing: although the film is unimaginable without the Needle, no acting scenes were filmed inside it. The tower sells the location; the drama happens elsewhere.

Television made the Needle a weekly establishing shot. Grey's Anatomy, filmed mostly in Los Angeles, flew crews to Seattle for exteriors, and the Space Needle features prominently as the backdrop of its outdoor scenes and skyline shots. Frasier's title sequence opens on the classic Kerry Park view: the Needle dead center against Elliott Bay and the Cascades, the postcard that tells viewers where they are in a single frame. For three decades that half-acre overlook has sold Seattle to audiences in seconds, which is why location managers keep booking it.

timeline.text: Hotel executive Edward E. Carlson sketches a saucer-topped tower on a napkin.
Construction starts at the Seattle Center.
The tower is completed after about 400 days of construction.
The Space Needle opens to the public on the first day of the Century 21 Exposition, the Seattle World's Fair.
Sleepless in Seattle makes the Needle a film pilgrimage site, though no acting scenes were shot inside it.
The city's Landmarks Preservation Board designates the tower a historic landmark.
Grey's Anatomy premieres and makes the Needle a weekly television establishing shot.
The Century Project renovation adds floor-to-ceiling glass and The Loupe, the world's first revolving glass floor.
